name: Byzantine Empire (Basil II)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 0.81 million km2 for 1000 CE (before Bulgaria) and 1.15 million km2 for 1050 CE. The historical-basemaps world_1000 polygons "Byzantine Empire" (0.84 million) + "Bulgar Khanate" (0.37 million, annexed 1018) measure 1.21 million km2 on the sphere, computed from the GeoJSON (mid).

population.note: Seshat (Byzantine Empire II) codes 10-14 million for 1000 CE, before the annexation of Bulgaria in 1018 (low). Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (isbn:0804726302, p. 570; via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_of_the_Byzantine_Empire, pointer) gives 12 million in 1025 (mid). High adds Bulgaria and the eastern annexations (Iberia, Vaspurakan, 1000-1022) to Seshat's upper value. Everything inside the border.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Constantinople (Seshat largest settlement 200,000-300,000, disputed, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/75) and Thessalonica; most towns were small kastra. Lower than the 6th century.

activePersonnel.note: Army: Haldon 1999 (Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World, p. 103) ~110,000 for 1025 (low); Madgearu 2013 (Byzantine Military Organization on the Danube, isbn:9789004252493, ch. II) cites an estimate of 250,000 (high, Treadgold's school); both via the manpower table at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_army (pointer). Mid army 160,000 between them. Navy: Treadgold (isbn:0804726302, p. 576, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_navy) puts oarsmen at 34,200 in 959 and 1025 plus up to 8,000 marines (supportPersonnel). Counted: tagmata (incl. the Varangian Guard), thematic soldiers on the military rolls (registered and paid, mustered seasonally), and the fleets. Allied Rus', Pecheneg and Armenian contingents are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Allied and mercenary contingents hired for campaigns (Rus', Pechenegs, Georgians, Armenian nobles) and thematic households not on the active rolls; militias of fortified towns.

supportPersonnel.note: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (p. 576) and Byzantium and Its Army (isbn:0804731632, p. 67) via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_navy (pointer): 34,200 oarsmen in 1025 and up to 8,000 marines at the 911 peak; mid 34,200 + ~4,000 imperial-fleet marines + staff. Low allows for the decline of the thematic fleets after 949 (Makrypoulias, as cited there).

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Thematic military lands obliged registered households to provide soldiers; an emergency call on all stratiotic households and militias could perhaps double or triple the registered army.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Army mid 160,000 (range 110,000-250,000, see activePersonnel) split ~70% infantry / 30% cavalry. Infantry split by the taxiarchy of the Praecepta Militaria (c. 965; McGeer, Sowing the Dragon's Teeth, isbn:0884022242): 400 hoplitai + 100 menaulatoi (line) + 300 archers + 200 light per 1,000 = 50/30/20. Includes the ~6,000 Varangians (sent by Vladimir in 988, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_army).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: lamellar or quilted armour, large shields, spears and menaulia; Varangians with axes and mail.

training.note: Tagmata and Varangians professional (0.75-1.0); thematic infantry part-time (0.5).

count.note: Archers = 30% of the infantry per the Praecepta Militaria taxiarchy; see infantry_line.

training.note: Thematic archers, drilled in the manuals' formations.

count.note: Javelinmen and slingers = 20% of the infantry per the Praecepta Militaria taxiarchy; see infantry_line.
Tagmata cavalry (Scholai, Exkoubitoi, Hikanatoi, Athanatoi and provincial tagmata) and thematic heavy horse including kataphraktoi; ~60-65% of the ~48,000 cavalry (30% of the 160,000 mid army).

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: kataphraktoi in lamellar with barded horses and maces, among the best heavy cavalry of the era.

training.note: Tagmata were full-time professionals under a strong drill tradition (rubric 0.75-1.0).

count.note: Thematic light horse, horse archers and scouts (trapezitai, prokoursatores); ~1/3 of the cavalry.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: lighter armour, bows and lances.

training.note: Border light horse experienced in raiding warfare (De velitatione).

count.note: Educated guess. Traction trebuchets (manganika), bolt-throwers on walls and siege trains of Basil II's Bulgarian campaigns; no count survives.

quality.note: Traction trebuchets and torsion bolt-throwers, era-typical to good.

training.note: Specialist engineers of the tagmata and themes.

count.note: Treadgold (Byzantium and Its Army, p. 85, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_navy, pointer) extrapolates ~240 warships for the 10th-century navy and 307 for the 960 Cretan expedition, probably the standing strength. Bireme dromons ~100 (the 960 fleet had 100 dromons + 200 chelandia per the same page).

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: bireme dromons with Greek fire siphons, the era's best war galleys.

training.note: Professional imperial fleet and marines; thematic fleets declining.

count.note: Chelandia, ousiakoi and galeai: the rest of Treadgold's ~240-307 warships (see ships_major).

quality.note: Lighter galleys, some with Greek fire.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: a trained officer corps working from military manuals (Praecepta, Taktika of Nikephoros Ouranos), proven commanders (Basil II, Ouranos, Xiphias) after half a century of victories.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.75 for the tagmata and Varangians; thematic levies of landholding soldiers lower; the revolts of Skleros and Phokas (976-989) showed aristocratic factionalism.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: motivated, decades of victories (conquest of Bulgaria 1018, Armenian annexations).

weapons.note: Between anchor 3 and anchor 4: traction trebuchets, Greek fire, composite bows, kontarion lances and maces; no crossbow until the 1090s.

armor.note: Near anchor 4 (plate-and-mail, barding): klibanion lamellar, mail, horse barding for the kataphraktoi.

ships.note: Anchor 4 (galleys) with bireme dromons and Greek fire siphons.

fortification.note: Theodosian walls and a network of kastra; near anchor 4 short of concentric castles.

logistics.note: Anchor 3-4: aplekta staging camps, thematic supply system and sea transport; granaries of the capital.

communications.note: Anchor 3-4: the beacon chain from Cilicia to Constantinople (9th c.) and the public post (dromos).

isr.note: Year anchor 3-4: organised border scouting and spies described in De velitatione.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true (2011 int$): Turkey 1000 CE = 768, Egypt 1000 CE = 956, Iraq 1000 CE = 1,307. Byzantine Anatolia and the Balkans were closest to the Turkey value; the capital, Greece and southern Italy were richer. Mid ~800.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. The army was paid partly in cash (roga) and partly through military lands; Basil II left a treasury surplus. State revenue perhaps 5-10% of output, the largest part going to the army.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy; silk, textiles, metalwork and shipbuilding concentrated in the capital and Thebes.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Thrace, Bithynia and the Balkans fed Constantinople; recovering agrarian economy in the 10th-11th centuries.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Surviving Roman roads (Via Egnatia, the military road across Anatolia to the eastern frontier) plus maintained routes; much reduced from antiquity.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Constantinople, Thessalonica, Abydos, Attaleia, Bari, Dyrrachium, Trebizond, Cherson, Corinth.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Coastal and Black Sea shipping of the capital's grain supply; Venetian and Amalfitan shipping not counted.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies carrying grain on pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot; Byzantine campaigns used prepared aplekta and seasonal campaigning.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.07-0.11 horses, mules, oxen and donkeys per inhabitant x population; imperial stud farms (metata) in Anatolia.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: fortified cities and kastra, local thematic supply and population support; Anatolian plateau and Taurus passes give depth.

notes: Snapshot = December 1025 at Basil II's death, the territorial peak of middle Byzantium (Bulgaria annexed 1018, Iberia and Vaspurakan 1000-1022). Force convention: activePersonnel = tagmata, Varangian Guard, thematic soldiers on the paid military rolls and the fleets; hired allied contingents in trainedReserves. Army size is genuinely disputed: Haldon ~110,000 vs Treadgold-type estimates of ~250,000 (Whittow argued for far fewer per unit); the mid 160,000 is between them and every P-role count inherits that spread. Haldon, Treadgold and Madgearu are cited by ISBN (not fetchable); their figures were read from Wikipedia tables (pointer only), hence grade B at most. Border = historical-basemaps world_1000 "Byzantine Empire" + "Bulgar Khanate" (Bulgaria annexed 1018). Ancient/medieval chroniclers are not used for counts.
